selection_reason: 1. Evidence: no experiments have been run yet, so we have no data on any design factor (modality, single vs. multi-profile, RNA encoder, image encoder, aggregation, fusion). 2. What this tests: config_036 is a central anchor. It is multimodal and multiprofile, which I expect to be competitive, and uses a mid-sized RNA encoder (scVI with 200 dimensions) and a strong image encoder (ImageNet ViT-L). It also uses the simplest aggregation (average pooling) and the simplest fusion (concatenation). This gives a reasonably strong first result without committing to the more complex transformer aggregation or weighted fusion. 3. Why it is the best use of the budget: later experiments can change one factor at a time from this anchor. That includes switching to RNA-only or image-only, to single-profile, to transformer aggregation, to weighted fusion, or to a different encoder. Each of these comparisons then isolates the effect of one design choice, which is more informative under a limited budget than starting from a minimal baseline far from the likely optimum.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: There is only one result so far. config_036 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI, ViT-L, avgpool, concat) reached 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. We do not yet know how much of this comes from the image branch versus the RNA branch. 2) What this tests: config_005 keeps everything the same except that it removes the image modality (RNA-only, scVI, multiprofile, avgpool). This one-factor change shows directly whether adding images improves on RNA alone. 3) Why now: Whether to use multimodal input is the decision with the widest consequences in this search space. Answering it first tells us whether to spend the remaining budget on fusion, image-encoder and aggregation variants, or on RNA-encoder choices. That makes it a better use of one experiment than fine-tuning secondary settings such as aggregation or fusion type.

Evidence: with the scvi_n200 RNA encoder and avgpool aggregation fixed, multimodal concat with imagenet_vit_l scored 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. RNA-only scored 0.650 accuracy and 0.628 F1, about 6.5 points lower. Uncertainty: we cannot yet tell whether this gain comes from combining the two modalities or simply from the image features alone. Test: image-only imagenet_vit_l with avgpool uses the same image encoder, profile setting and aggregation, so it completes the RNA-only, image-only and multimodal comparison. If image-only is close to 0.715, RNA adds little, and future runs should focus on image encoders and aggregation rather than RNA encoders or fusion. If it is clearly lower, the two modalities are complementary, and tuning fusion, aggregation and RNA encoder within multimodal configurations is justified. Why now: this question decides which design dimensions deserve the remaining budget, so it is a better use of one experiment than a single-dimension tweak of the current best.

1) Evidence: the multimodal model (config_036, scVI + ViT-L, avgpool, concat) scored best at 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. RNA-only reached 0.650 and image-only only 0.332, so the RNA signal carries most of the performance and the image adds a meaningful amount on top. Every run so far used avgpool, so we do not know whether aggregation matters. That is a major untested design axis for multiprofile inputs. 2) Test: config_038 changes only avgpool to transformer and keeps the rest of the best configuration fixed. This isolates whether learned, attention-based aggregation across profiles beats simple mean pooling. 3) Why now: it is a one-factor exploitation of the current best direction, so the result is directly interpretable as an aggregation effect. If the transformer helps, it becomes the new base for later tests of the RNA encoder (scGPT, PCA) and the fusion method (weighted). If it does not, we can confidently use the cheaper avgpool for the rest of the budget.

1. Evidence: multimodal models (about 0.715 to 0.721 accuracy) clearly beat RNA-only (0.650) and image-only (0.332). RNA is therefore the dominant signal and images add a useful complement. Aggregation looks like a minor factor: transformer beat avgpool by about 0.006 in accuracy, but avgpool had slightly higher F1, so the result is inconclusive. The RNA encoder has never been varied (only scvi_n200 tested), and RNA carries most of the predictive signal, so this is the largest untested source of uncertainty. 2. This experiment keeps the best multimodal setup (multiprofile, imagenet_vit_l, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) and swaps scvi_n200 for scGPT. Any change can then be attributed to the RNA encoder alone. 3. Under a limited budget, this tests the design choice most likely to move performance substantially and stays within the promising multimodal region. Fusion type and image encoder are worth testing later, but they likely have smaller effects given that the image modality is weak.

1. Evidence: multimodal scVI plus ViT-L is the clear best direction, at about 0.715–0.721 accuracy. It beats RNA-only (0.650) by a wide margin, while image-only is weak (0.332). Avgpool and transformer aggregation are nearly tied: transformer is slightly higher on accuracy, avgpool slightly higher on F1, so aggregation looks minor. scGPT clearly underperforms scVI. Fusion strategy has never been tested; every multimodal run so far used concat. 2. This experiment keeps the best-performing setup (scVI, ViT-L, multiprofile, transformer) and swaps concat for weighted fusion. That isolates the effect of fusion directly. Weighted fusion is a plausible improvement here because the image modality is much weaker than RNA, and learned modality weighting could down-weight noisy image features. 3. Why this is the best use of the budget: it builds on the strongest region of the search space and resolves an entirely unexplored design axis with a single controlled comparison. The result will tell us whether fusion should be fixed or explored further before spending runs on secondary axes such as the image encoder or PCA features.

1) Evidence: RNA is the dominant modality. RNA-only scvi reached 0.650, while image-only ViT-L reached only 0.332. The RNA encoder choice has the largest observed effect: swapping scvi for scGPT dropped accuracy from about 0.72 to 0.51. Aggregation and fusion changes within scvi+ViT-L produced only small gains (0.715 to 0.725), and F1 moved inconsistently, so those are fine-tuning details rather than major levers. pca_n2000 is the one RNA encoder never tested. 2) This experiment swaps only the RNA encoder to pca_n2000 in the current best setup (ViT-L, multiprofile, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion). Comparing it directly with config_039 shows whether scvi is truly the best RNA representation or whether a simpler, higher-dimensional PCA input works as well or better. 3) Because the RNA encoder has the largest demonstrated impact and pca_n2000 is a complete unknown, this test reduces the most important remaining uncertainty. It also has a realistic chance of beating the current best. Testing resnet50 or singleprofile can come next, since the image branch contributes less.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: The broad choices look settled. scVI beats scGPT and PCA, multiprofile beats singleprofile, and multimodal beats RNA-only and image-only. Within the top region (scVI + ViT-L, multiprofile), the remaining choices show only small, single-run gaps. avgpool+concat scored 0.715, transformer+concat 0.721 and transformer+weighted 0.725, with F1 roughly flat at 0.681-0.687. This separates the effect of aggregation from the effect of fusion and shows whether they interact. If avgpool+weighted roughly matches transformer+weighted, the costlier transformer aggregation is not clearly justified, and fusion becomes the more important lever. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: It is a low-risk, high-information follow-up in the most promising region, so it can also produce a top result. Settling these two design questions before spending budget on other comparisons, such as ResNet50 vs ViT-L, avoids misreading small differences.

What this tests: config_031 (scVI, ResNet50, avgpool, weighted) varies only the aggregation relative to config_033. 1) No experiments have been run, so there is no evidence yet on any design factor: modality, single vs. multi-profile, RNA encoder, image encoder, aggregation or fusion. 2) config_030 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI RNA encoder, ResNet50 image encoder, avgpool aggregation, concat fusion) sits near the middle of the design space and is a reasonable guess at a strong configuration. 1. Evidence and uncertainty: only one experiment is complete. config_030 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200 + resnet50, avgpool, concat) reached 0.632 accuracy and 0.607 F1. 1. Evidence: The RNA-only scVI avgpool model (0.650 acc, 0.628 F1) beats the matched multimodal scVI+ResNet50 concat model (0.632 acc, 0.607 F1). Test: Swap scVI for the scGPT foundation-model embedding while keeping the current best setup fixed (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool). 1) Evidence: scvi_n200 is the strongest RNA encoder so far. Its RNA-only avgpool run (0.650 acc, 0.628 F1) clearly beats scGPT (0.530). Evidence: scvi_n200 is clearly the better RNA encoder so far (about 0.65 accuracy vs 0.53 for scgpt). Transformer and avgpool aggregation perform almost the same (0.653 vs 0.650). 1) Evidence: scVI is clearly the strongest RNA encoder tested (about 0.65 vs 0.53 for scGPT). Weighted fusion beat concat in the multimodal setting (0.678 vs 0.632 accuracy, with F1 agreeing). 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Weighted fusion beat concat (0.678 vs 0.632 with resnet50). ViT-L beat resnet50 (0.706 vs 0.678). 1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_039 (scVI + ViT-L, transformer, weighted, 0.725 accuracy / 0.685 F1). The best RNA-only run reaches about 0.653. 1. Evidence: All nine experiments so far used multiprofile inputs. The best result is config_039 (scVI, ViT-L, transformer, weighted) at 0.725 acc / 0.685 F1. Across encoders and fusion types, scVI beats PCA and scGPT, ViT-L beats ResNet50, and weighted fusion beats concat. 1) No experiments have been run yet, so nothing is known about which design choices matter: modality (RNA, image, or both), single vs. multi-profile, encoder choice, aggregation, or fusion. 2) config_018 is a central baseline that sits in the middle of most axes. 1. Evidence: there is only one result so far. The multimodal, multiprofile config_018 (PCA + ResNet50, avgpool, concat) reached 0.619 accuracy and 0.610 F1. Test: config_002 is the matched RNA-only ablation. It uses the same PCA encoder, multiprofile setting and avgpool aggregation, and drops only the image branch. Running it early avoids spending many runs on a dimension that may not matter.

1) Evidence: with all other settings fixed (multiprofile, PCA RNA, avgpool), adding ResNet50 images with concat fusion raised accuracy from 0.591 to 0.619 and F1 from 0.573 to 0.610. 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Multimodal fusion beats RNA-only by about 3-4 points in accuracy (0.619 and 0.629 vs 0.591), so multimodal multiprofile is the promising region. 1. Evidence and uncertainty: switching the RNA encoder to scVI gave the largest gain so far, with config_036 reaching 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. Concat and weighted fusion perform similarly. 1. Evidence: Switching the RNA encoder from PCA to scVI gave by far the largest gain (about 0.63 to 0.71). Evidence: scVI is clearly the strongest RNA encoder, since swapping in scGPT or PCA dropped accuracy by 14 to 20 points. This one run resolves the largest attribution uncertainty in the search, which makes it a better use of budget than a marginal tweak to the current best.

1. Evidence: the best result so far is config_037 (scVI + ViT-L, avgpool, weighted; 0.706 acc / 0.667 F1). 1. Evidence/uncertainty: no experiments have been run, so we do not yet know whether multimodal fusion, multiprofile aggregation, or encoder choice matters most. 2. 1. Evidence: only two runs exist. RNA-only scVI with avgpool (0.650 accuracy, 0.628 F1) slightly beat multimodal scVI + ResNet50 with concat (0.632, 0.607). Why now: the RNA encoder is a three-level choice that affects every multimodal configuration, and it is currently fully unexplored. 1. Evidence and uncertainty: scVI clearly beats scGPT as the RNA encoder (0.650 vs 0.530 accuracy, same setup). Evidence: scVI is clearly the best RNA encoder so far (about 0.65 vs 0.53 for scGPT). The choice between transformer and avgpool aggregation barely matters (0.653 vs 0.650). Adding ResNet50 image features by concatenation (config_030) slightly lowered accuracy and F1 compared with RNA-only (0.632 vs 0.650). 1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_031 (multimodal, scVI, ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion; acc 0.678, F1 0.646). 1. Evidence: Weighted fusion clearly beat concat (0.678 vs 0.632 with resnet50). Test: config_039 changes only the aggregation (avgpool to transformer) relative to the current best. It isolates whether learned aggregation helps once both modalities are fused. 3. 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_039 (scVI + ViT-L, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion), with accuracy 0.725 and F1 0.685. 1. Evidence and uncertainty: the best result so far is config_039 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion; 0.725 accuracy, 0.685 F1). 1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_039 (scVI + ViT-L, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. 1) No experiments have been run yet, so we know nothing about which modality, encoder, aggregation or fusion choice matters. 2) This multimodal, multiprofile run uses the simplest options on every axis: PCA RNA features, ResNet50 image features, average pooling and concatenation fusion. 1. Evidence: Only one experiment has been run (config_018: multimodal, multiprofile, PCA RNA, ResNet50, avgpool, concat; val acc 0.619, F1 0.610). 1) Evidence: Two runs so far, both multimodal, multiprofile, PCA RNA, avgpool and concat. They differ only in image encoder. 1) Evidence: The three runs all used multiprofile, avgpool and concat. PCA_n2000 clearly beat scGPT (about 0.63 vs 0.52 accuracy with the ViT-L image encoder). 1) Evidence so far: the RNA encoder choice matters a lot. PCA_n2000 beat scGPT by about 0.11 accuracy with the same ViT-L, avgpool and concat setup. Fine-tuning fusion or aggregation around config_037 would likely give small, noisy differences. 1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_037 (scVI + ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion), with accuracy 0.706 and F1 0.667. This beats RNA-only scVI (0.650), so adding images helps. Evidence: the best result so far is config_037 (scVI + ViT-L, avgpool, weighted fusion), at 0.706 accuracy and 0.667 F1. Evidence: the best result so far is config_037 (scVI + ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion; acc 0.706, F1 0.667). scVI clearly beats PCA and scGPT, and ViT-L edges out ResNet50. Aggregation is the main open question. Transformer aggregation was tested only once, in the weaker PCA + ViT-L + concat setting, where it scored about 3 points below avgpool. These choices are modality (RNA, image, or both), single vs. multi profile, RNA encoder, image encoder, aggregation and fusion. 2) What this tests: config_030 is a central anchor point. 1) Evidence: there is only one result so far. Multimodal scVI + ResNet50 with avgpool and concat fusion reached 0.632 accuracy and 0.607 F1. With only two runs, it is unclear whether images add little signal or whether naive concatenation lets noisy image features dilute the stronger RNA signal. 2. Test: config_031 changes only concat to weighted fusion and keeps the encoders and aggregation fixed. It isolates whether a learned modality weighting can recover or exceed RNA-only performance. 3. Why now: whether to fuse modalities at all is a high-level decision that shapes much of the remaining search space. Test: config_033 keeps the best configuration (config_031) fixed and changes only avgpool to transformer aggregation. Any difference can then be attributed to aggregation alone. 3. Why now: This builds directly on the best result while answering an open structural question. A transformer gain would point toward a stronger family of configurations. 1) Evidence: every run so far used the scvi_n200 RNA encoder. Within that set, weighted fusion beat concat (0.678 vs 0.632 with avgpool), and transformer aggregation beat avgpool (0.713 vs 0.678). 1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_039 (scVI + ViT-L + transformer + weighted, 0.725 acc). Swapping only the RNA encoder to scGPT (config_051) dropped accuracy to 0.520. 1) Evidence: scVI is clearly the strongest RNA encoder (scGPT reached 0.520 and PCA 0.586 versus 0.725 for scVI in the same setup). Weighted fusion beat concat once with avgpool (0.678 vs 0.632). Transformer aggregation beat avgpool once (0.713 vs 0.678). The current best is config_039 (scVI + ViT-L + transformer + weighted, 0.725 accuracy). Every experiment so far has used the multiprofile setting, so the singleprofile/multiprofile choice is completely untested. 2) Test: config_035 keeps the best encoders and weighted fusion but switches to singleprofile, which has no aggregation. That is the core design question in this study. 3) Why now: a whole design dimension has no evidence, which is the largest remaining uncertainty. Evidence: multiprofile clearly beats singleprofile (0.537 for config_035 vs 0.725 for config_039). scVI is the strongest RNA encoder, well ahead of PCA (0.586) and scGPT (0.520). Transformer aggregation beats avgpool (0.713 vs 0.678), and weighted fusion beats concat (0.678 vs 0.632). The value of the image modality is still unclear. The only RNA-only run (config_005, avgpool, 0.650) is close to the multimodal avgpool runs (0.632 to 0.678). All the large gains have come alongside transformer aggregation, which has never been tried without images. Question: config_006 (RNA-only, scVI, multiprofile, transformer) separates the effect of the transformer aggregator from the effect of adding images. If it scores close to 0.71–0.72, the image branch adds little, and the rest of the budget should go to RNA and aggregation choices. If it scores well below that, multimodal fusion is confirmed as necessary, and further image-encoder and fusion tuning (e.g., config_038) is justified. Why now: this single ablation addresses the most consequential unresolved design choice, whether to use multiple modalities at all. That makes it more informative than another small variation around the current best.

Evidence: multiprofile scVI with weighted fusion and transformer aggregation is the strongest region so far. config_039 (ViT-L) reached 0.725 accuracy and config_033 (ResNet50) reached 0.713. RNA-only scVI sits near 0.65 regardless of aggregation. Swapping the RNA encoder to scGPT or PCA in the ViT-L multimodal model dropped accuracy sharply (0.52 and 0.59). However, no image-only model has been tested, so we cannot tell how much of the multimodal gain comes from the image branch versus true fusion. We also cannot explain why weaker RNA encoders drag performance so far below what ViT-L features might reach alone. Test: the ViT-L, multiprofile, transformer image-only model is the direct unimodal counterpart of the current best configuration. If it nears 0.72, the RNA branch adds little and future effort should go to the image side and fusion robustness. If it is much lower, that confirms real complementarity and justifies exploiting the scVI multimodal setup, for example with fusion variants. Why now: this single run fills the largest gap in the design space, the image-only modality, and anchors interpretation of every multimodal result. That makes it more informative than another small fusion tweak near the current best.

1. Evidence: No experiments have been run, so we have no information yet on any design axis (modality, single vs. multi-profile, RNA encoder, image encoder, aggregation, fusion). 2. What it tests: config_030 is multimodal and multiprofile, with mid-range choices on the other axes: scvi_n200 for RNA, resnet50 for images, avgpool aggregation and concat fusion. These are simple, low-variance defaults, so the result is a reliable anchor for the full pipeline. From there, each later experiment can change one factor at a time. Dropping a modality (config_005 or config_011) or switching to single-profile (config_028) would show whether multimodality and multiple profiles help. Swapping to transformer aggregation, weighted fusion, scGPT or ViT-L would show which of those upgrades matter. 3. Why now: Starting from the cheapest baseline (rna_only, PCA) would tell us little about the large multimodal part of the search space. A central anchor gives a reasonable chance of good early performance, and every later comparison becomes an informative single-factor test. That is the most efficient use of a limited budget.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: there is only one result so far. config_030 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI + ResNet50, avgpool, concat) reached 0.632 accuracy and 0.607 F1. One point cannot tell us which components drive that performance. The most basic open question is whether the image modality adds anything over RNA alone. 2. What this tests: config_005 is the same setup with the image branch removed (RNA-only, multiprofile, scVI, avgpool). Because only one factor changes, the accuracy and F1 gap directly measures the image contribution. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: the answer decides where later experiments should go. If images help clearly, it is worth comparing image encoders (ViT-L vs ResNet50) and fusion methods. If they add little, the budget is better spent on RNA encoders (scGPT, PCA) and aggregation. This makes it a more useful experiment than a local tweak of fusion or aggregation.

Evidence: with scVI RNA features and avgpool aggregation, adding ResNet50 image features via concat fusion scored 0.632 accuracy and 0.607 F1. The RNA-only version scored 0.650 and 0.628, so adding images gave no gain and possibly a small loss. It is unclear whether the image features add little, or whether naive concatenation dilutes the RNA signal with noisy image dimensions. What this tests: config_031 keeps everything the same as config_030 but switches to weighted fusion. That isolates the fusion choice and shows whether a learned modality weighting can recover or beat RNA-only performance. Why now: this is a clean one-factor comparison. Its answer decides whether the large multimodal part of the search space (most remaining configs) is worth pursuing. It also tells us which fusion type to carry forward before testing encoders and aggregation.

1) Evidence: with scVI-n200 RNA, ResNet50 images, multiprofile input and avgpool, weighted fusion (0.678 acc, 0.646 F1) beat both RNA-only (0.650) and concat fusion (0.632). Weighted fusion looks like the right way to add images, but this rests on only three runs. Aggregation has never been varied: every run so far used avgpool. 2) This run keeps the current best setup (config_031) and swaps avgpool for transformer aggregation. It tests whether learned attention across profiles improves on simple averaging under the best fusion found so far. 3) It is a single-factor change from the leading configuration, so any difference can be attributed to aggregation. That makes it useful as exploitation, since it could beat the current best, and as exploration, since it settles a key untested design choice. Image encoder (ViT-L) and RNA encoder (scGPT) changes can follow once aggregation is understood.

Evidence: with the scvi_n200 + resnet50 backbone, weighted fusion beat concat under avgpool (0.678 vs 0.632). Transformer aggregation then beat avgpool under weighted fusion (0.713 vs 0.678). F1 shows the same pattern both times. Fusion and aggregation therefore have reasonable support, but the encoder choices are still completely untested: every multimodal run used resnet50 and scvi_n200. The image encoder is a major design axis, and a stronger pretrained ViT-L could plausibly give large gains. This experiment changes only the image encoder (resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l) from the current best (config_033) and keeps transformer aggregation and weighted fusion. It isolates the effect of image representation quality in the strongest known setting. It exploits the best configuration while removing the biggest remaining uncertainty, so it is the most informative use of the limited budget.

1) Evidence: All five runs so far used the scvi_n200 RNA encoder. Within that setting, weighted fusion beat concat (0.678 vs 0.632) and transformer aggregation beat avgpool (0.713 vs 0.678). ViT-L edged out ResNet50 on accuracy (0.725 vs 0.713), but its F1 was slightly lower, so the image-encoder difference is small and uncertain. The RNA encoder choice is completely untested, which is the largest gap in what we know. 2) This run keeps the best-known setup (multiprofile, ViT-L, transformer, weighted) and swaps only the RNA encoder to scGPT. Any change in accuracy can then be attributed to the RNA encoder alone. 3) It is the best use of the next run because it explores the most important untested factor, and doing so inside the strongest configuration also gives a realistic chance of beating the current best of 0.725. If scGPT underperforms, that supports keeping scvi_n200 and moving to PCA or to finer refinements next.

1. Evidence: Weighted fusion beat concat (0.678 vs 0.632 under avgpool), and transformer aggregation beat avgpool (0.713 vs 0.678). ViT-L and ResNet50 were close: ViT-L had higher accuracy (0.725 vs 0.713) but slightly lower F1, so the image encoder looks like a minor factor. The RNA encoder had by far the largest effect: swapping scVI for scGPT dropped accuracy from 0.725 to 0.520. Yet pca_n2000, the third RNA option, has never been tested. 2. Test: config_027 keeps the best pipeline (ViT-L, transformer, weighted, multiprofile) and changes only the RNA encoder to PCA. This isolates whether scVI is truly the best RNA representation or whether a simpler PCA input matches or beats it. 3. Why now: RNA encoder choice is the design decision with the most impact and the most remaining uncertainty. Testing it in the strongest known context reduces that uncertainty efficiently and could also produce a new best configuration.

1) Evidence: scVI is clearly the best RNA encoder; scGPT (0.520) and PCA (0.586) fall well behind it in the best pipeline. Weighted fusion beat concat (0.678 vs 0.632 with avgpool). Transformer aggregation beat avgpool (0.713 vs 0.678 with ResNet50). The current best is config_039 (scVI + ViT-L + transformer + weighted, 0.725), only about 1 point above ResNet50 (0.713). The open uncertainty is how much images actually add. RNA-only scVI with avgpool (0.650) beat multimodal concat (0.632) and was only about 3 points below weighted multimodal avgpool. The only RNA-only baseline uses avgpool, so part of the multimodal gain may come from transformer aggregation rather than from the image modality. 2) This experiment: RNA-only scVI with transformer aggregation (config_006) matches the top configurations on RNA encoder, profile setting and aggregation, and removes the image branch. That isolates the image contribution. If it reaches about 0.70 or more, the multimodal benefit is small and the search should focus on aggregation and RNA design. If it stays well below 0.71, image fusion is confirmed as a key driver. 3) Why now: further fusion or image-encoder tweaks would mostly refine a nearly settled region. This ablation resolves the most important open design question, whether multimodality matters, in a single run, so it is the best use of limited budget.

1) Evidence: scvi_n200 is clearly the strongest RNA encoder, beating pca_n2000 (0.586) and scgpt (0.520) under the same setup. Weighted fusion beat concat with avgpool (0.678 vs 0.632). Transformer aggregation beat avgpool (0.713 vs 0.678). The best result so far is config_039 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) at 0.725 accuracy. However, every experiment so far has used multiprofile, so the profile-setting axis is completely unexplored. 2) This run keeps the best-performing encoders and weighted fusion but switches to singleprofile, where aggregation is not applicable. It tests directly whether multiprofile aggregation drives the gains, or whether a simpler single-profile model performs comparably. 3) This is the largest remaining uncertainty about an important design choice. One run will show whether the multiprofile assumption behind the whole search is justified. That is more informative than small refinements near the current best, such as concat vs weighted with a transformer, where evidence already favors weighted.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_039 (scVI + ViT-L, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) at 0.725 accuracy. RNA-only baselines with scVI sit at about 0.65 under both aggregations. Transformer aggregation and weighted fusion each look helpful, but each rests on a single comparison. No image-only experiment has been run, so we cannot tell how much of the multimodal gain comes from the image branch versus true fusion of both modalities. 2. What this tests: config_015 is the image-only counterpart of the best configuration (ViT-L, multiprofile, transformer). If it reaches about 0.72, the RNA branch adds little and further search should focus on image encoders and aggregation. If it falls well below, that confirms real complementary multimodal value and justifies refining fusion and the RNA encoder. 3. Why this is the best next experiment: It resolves a major untested design dimension (modality setting) with a single run. It does so directly against the current best, which makes its result more informative than a small fusion or aggregation tweak to a configuration that already scores well.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so every design choice is unresolved: modality, single vs multi-profile, encoder choice, aggregation and fusion. 2) What this tests: config_018 is a central baseline for the full multimodal pipeline. It uses the simplest component on each axis: PCA RNA features, ResNet50 image features, multi-profile avgpool aggregation and concat fusion. This gives a reference point for the search space. Later single-factor changes can then be compared against it, such as dropping a modality (config_002 / config_011), switching to single-profile (config_016), or swapping in transformer aggregation, weighted fusion, scGPT/scVI or ViT-L. 3) Why now: Starting from a simple, middle-of-the-space configuration lets each later experiment work as a controlled ablation. That should reveal which factors matter with the fewest runs. It also has a reasonable chance of performing well, since it combines both modalities and multiple profiles, while avoiding the extra variance that more complex components could add.

1. Evidence: Only one experiment has been run. config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA RNA, ResNet50, avgpool, concat) reached 0.619 accuracy and 0.610 F1. That gives a baseline but no evidence yet about which design choices matter. 2. What this tests: config_024 is identical except that it swaps ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L. This isolates the effect of the image encoder, which is likely one of the most influential choices because it sets the quality of the image representation every fused model depends on. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: A one-factor change against the baseline gives a clean comparison. The result will tell us which image backbone to carry forward in later RNA-encoder, aggregation and fusion experiments, so it narrows a large part of the remaining search space. It is also plausibly a better-performing configuration, so it serves both learning and optimization.

1) Evidence: Two runs so far differ only in the image encoder (ResNet50 vs ImageNet ViT-L, both with PCA RNA, multiprofile, avgpool and concat). ViT-L gained about 0.010 in accuracy but lost about 0.011 in F1, so the image encoder looks like a minor factor and remains unresolved. The RNA encoder, aggregation and fusion choices are completely untested. 2) Test: This run changes only the RNA encoder, from PCA-2000 to scVI-200, keeping everything else as in the best-accuracy run (ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, concat). It isolates the effect of the RNA representation. 3) Why now: The RNA encoder is likely a high-impact design choice, and a clean single-factor comparison against config_024 makes the result easy to interpret. It also stays close to the current best region, so it may improve performance as well as reduce uncertainty.

1) Evidence: The RNA encoder is the strongest lever seen so far. Switching from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200, with ViT-L, avgpool and concat held fixed, raised accuracy from 0.629 to 0.715 and F1 from 0.599 to 0.687. By comparison, switching the image encoder from resnet50 to ViT-L changed accuracy by only about 1 point and slightly lowered F1. The third RNA encoder option, scgpt, has not been tested, nor have transformer aggregation or weighted fusion. 2) Test: config_048 changes only the RNA encoder of the current best setup (scvi_n200 to scgpt), so any difference is attributable to that choice. It shows whether a foundation-model RNA embedding beats scvi, which would shift the best region, or confirms scvi as the RNA encoder to build on. 3) Why now: The RNA encoder is the only factor with clear evidence of large effects, and a third of its options are still unexplored. Settling it before tuning smaller choices like aggregation and fusion keeps later experiments anchored on the right encoder.

1) Evidence: Across the four multimodal runs, the RNA encoder is the dominant factor. With ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool and concat held fixed, scvi_n200 reached 0.715 accuracy, versus 0.629 for pca_n2000 and 0.518 for scgpt, and F1 follows the same ranking. Swapping the image encoder (resnet50 vs ViT-L with PCA) changed accuracy by only about 1 point, and F1 slightly favoured resnet50, so that choice looks secondary. Aggregation, fusion and the singleprofile setting have not been tested at all. 2) This run keeps the best setup (scvi_n200 + ViT-L, multiprofile, concat) and changes only avgpool to transformer aggregation, a clean single-factor test. 3) Aggregation is probably the largest remaining untested architectural choice for multiprofile data. Testing it on the strongest backbone could directly raise the best result while also answering a key design question. Fusion (config_037) and unimodal baselines can follow once aggregation is understood.

1) Evidence: The RNA encoder matters most so far. scvi_n200 (~0.715–0.721 accuracy) clearly beats pca_n2000 (~0.62–0.63) and scgpt (~0.52). The two aggregation settings with scvi+ViT-L are nearly tied: transformer has slightly higher accuracy (0.721 vs 0.715) but slightly lower F1 (0.681 vs 0.687), so that choice is unresolved. Fusion is the largest unknown, because every run so far used concat. 2) This experiment swaps concat for weighted fusion in the current best setup (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer, multiprofile). It isolates the effect of fusion where performance is highest. 3) Under a limited budget, this both explores an untested design axis and exploits the strongest region found so far. It could produce a new best, and a null result would still show whether fusion choice needs more budget.

1) Evidence: The RNA encoder is clearly the dominant factor. scVI reaches about 0.72 accuracy, while PCA reaches about 0.62 and scGPT about 0.52. Within the scVI + ViT-L setting, aggregation and fusion changes produced only small, uncertain gains (0.715 to 0.725). The image encoder has only been compared under the weaker PCA backbone. There, ViT-L had slightly higher accuracy (0.629 vs 0.619) but ResNet50 had higher F1 (0.610 vs 0.599), so that comparison is inconclusive. 2) Test: config_033 keeps the current best setup (scVI, multiprofile, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) and swaps only the image encoder to ResNet50. This isolates the image-encoder effect in the strong-RNA regime, where it may behave differently than with PCA. 3) Why this is the best use of the budget: further aggregation or fusion tweaks are unlikely to move results much. The image encoder is the main untested design choice in the best context. Testing it could either produce a new best configuration or confirm ViT-L as the better choice, so it is both informative and has reasonable upside.

1) Evidence: The RNA encoder is the dominant factor so far. scVI scored about 0.71-0.72 accuracy, PCA about 0.62-0.63 and scGPT about 0.52. In contrast, swapping the image encoder (resnet50 vs ViT-L, 0.713 vs 0.725), aggregation (transformer vs avgpool, about +0.006) and fusion (weighted vs concat, about +0.004) produced only small shifts, close to noise. All seven runs were multimodal, so it is untested whether the image branch contributes at all. 2) Test: An RNA-only scVI model with multiprofile transformer aggregation is a direct ablation of the best runs (config_038 and config_039) with the image modality removed. If it matches about 0.72, imaging adds little and the remaining budget should shift toward RNA-side and profile-setting choices. If it drops clearly, the multimodal gain is confirmed, and finer tuning of image encoder and fusion is justified. 3) Why now: Further small fusion or aggregation tweaks within the scVI multimodal family are unlikely to be distinguishable from noise. This ablation resolves the most important open design question, whether multimodality matters, with a single experiment.

1) Evidence: scVI is clearly the best RNA encoder, at about 0.71-0.72 accuracy, versus about 0.62 for PCA and 0.52 for scGPT. Adding images to scVI also helps: multimodal reaches 0.725 versus 0.653 for RNA-only. Aggregation, fusion and image-encoder choices have produced only small differences of about 0.01 or less. The main uncertainty is the profile setting: every experiment so far used multiprofile, so we have no evidence on how much multiprofile aggregation contributes. 2) This experiment takes the current best setup (scVI + ViT-L, weighted fusion) and switches it to singleprofile, keeping the other components fixed. This isolates the effect of multiprofile aggregation. The comparison is with config_039 (0.725) and, more loosely, the avgpool and transformer variants (config_036 and config_038). 3) Further fine-tuning of aggregation or fusion is likely to give only marginal gains. Testing a design axis that has never been tried is the most informative use of the budget. It tells us whether multiprofile matters or whether a simpler singleprofile model performs about as well.

1. Evidence: The main design choices look settled. scvi_n200 is the clear best RNA encoder (about 0.72 accuracy, versus about 0.63 for pca_n2000 and 0.52 for scgpt). Multiprofile beats singleprofile by a wide margin (0.725 vs 0.537). Among the top scvi multiprofile runs, image encoder, aggregation and fusion change accuracy by only about 1 point (0.713 to 0.725), which is likely within noise. The modality question is only half answered. RNA-only scored 0.653, below multimodal at 0.725, but no image-only run exists, so we do not know how much the image branch contributes on its own. 2. Test: config_015 is image-only with imagenet_vit_l and transformer aggregation in the multiprofile setting. This matches the RNA-only run (config_006) and the best multimodal run (config_039), giving a clean three-way modality ablation. It will show whether images are a strong standalone signal or mainly complementary to RNA. 3. Why now: further small fusion or aggregation tweaks around the best configuration are unlikely to separate meaningfully from noise. Resolving the image modality's role reduces uncertainty about a major design choice and helps decide whether remaining budget should go to image-side variants.

1) No experiments have been run yet, so there is no evidence on whether multimodal fusion, multiprofile aggregation, or any particular encoder matters. 2) config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA RNA + ResNet50 image, avgpool aggregation, concat fusion) is a central anchor. It pairs the simplest encoders with the simplest aggregation and fusion choices, and it touches the two highest-level design axes: using both modalities and pooling multiple profiles. Later experiments can then each change one factor from this point: drop to a single modality, switch to single-profile, swap one encoder for scVI, scGPT or ViT-L, or use transformer aggregation or weighted fusion. Each such change would isolate the effect of that design decision. 3) A moderately expressive but low-complexity configuration gives a reasonable chance of strong performance while keeping the clearest attribution for later one-factor comparisons. That makes it a better first use of a limited budget than starting at an extreme, such as the simplest unimodal model or the most complex foundation-model plus transformer setup.

1) Evidence and uncertainty: only one experiment has been run. config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000 + resnet50, avgpool, concat) reached 0.619 accuracy and 0.610 F1. That gives a baseline but says nothing yet about which design choices matter. 2) What this tests: config_024 changes only the image encoder, from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l, and keeps every other setting fixed. Any difference can therefore be attributed to the image backbone. 3) Why it is the best next use of budget: encoder choice is plausibly one of the largest sources of variation, and the image encoder appears in many of the remaining configurations. Settling it early will narrow the search space more than testing smaller factors such as fusion or aggregation first. It also has a reasonable chance of improving the best result so far.

1. Evidence: Swapping resnet50 for imagenet_vit_l under pca_n2000, multiprofile, avgpool and concat gave a small, mixed result. Accuracy rose about 0.01 (0.629 vs 0.619) while F1 fell about 0.011. The image encoder therefore looks like a weak lever, and the other factors (RNA encoder, aggregation, fusion) are still completely untested. 2. Test: This run keeps the current best setup (multiprofile, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat) and changes only the RNA encoder from pca_n2000 to the pretrained scGPT embedding. It isolates whether the RNA representation, a three-level factor likely to drive large differences, matters more than the image backbone. 3. Why now: Changing one variable from the best configuration keeps the result interpretable. It reduces uncertainty about a high-impact, multi-level design choice rather than refining a factor that has already shown little effect. It also has a reasonable chance of improving on the best accuracy so far.

1) Evidence: The RNA encoder matters a lot. PCA beat scGPT by about 0.11 accuracy with the image encoder held fixed (0.629 vs 0.518). The image encoder difference is small and inconsistent: ViT-L has slightly higher accuracy, while ResNet50 has higher F1. So the image encoder is not yet a decisive factor. Aggregation has never been varied; every run so far used avgpool with concat fusion. 2) This experiment keeps the best-performing setup (PCA, ViT-L, multiprofile, concat) and changes only avgpool to transformer aggregation. That isolates whether learned attention over multiple profiles beats simple averaging. 3) Aggregation is a major untested design axis. Testing it on the strongest base both checks for an immediate gain and tells us which aggregation to carry forward. That is more informative than repeating the inconclusive image-encoder comparison or exploring the scGPT branch, which already looks weaker.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: Across four runs, the pca_n2000 RNA encoder clearly beat scgpt (0.629 vs 0.518 accuracy). Avgpool beat transformer aggregation in one paired comparison. ResNet50 and ViT-L performed similarly (0.619 vs 0.629 accuracy, with ResNet50 slightly higher on F1). Fusion strategy has never been varied, since every run used concat, so it is the largest untested design choice within the promising region. 2. What this tests: config_025 keeps the current best setup (pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, multiprofile, avgpool) and changes only the fusion to weighted. This isolates whether learned modality weighting helps beyond simple concatenation. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: it exploits the strongest known configuration while answering an open design question in a clean paired comparison. A gain would directly improve the best result. A loss would settle concat as the default and let later experiments go to the scvi_n200 encoder or unimodal ablations.

1) Evidence: The RNA encoder is the largest effect seen so far. Swapping pca_n2000 for scgpt cut accuracy by about 11 points (0.629 to 0.518). The other choices made only small differences. ViT-L was about 1 point better than ResNet50 on accuracy, but its F1 was lower. Avgpool beat transformer by about 3 points. Weighted fusion beat concat by about 0.7 points in accuracy and 1.9 points in F1. scvi_n200, the third RNA encoder, has never been tested. 2) Test: This run keeps the current best setup (multiprofile, ViT-L, avgpool, weighted fusion) and swaps only the RNA encoder to scvi_n200. That isolates whether scvi_n200 can match or beat PCA. 3) Rationale: Since the RNA encoder is the most influential factor, an untried option there is the biggest remaining uncertainty. This run either finds a better encoder or confirms PCA, using the strongest known settings so the result also has a real chance of a new best score. Single-profile and unimodal baselines can come later.

Evidence: the best result so far is config_037 (scVI RNA, ViT-L image, avgpool, weighted fusion) at 0.706 accuracy and 0.667 F1. Swapping PCA for scVI raised accuracy by about 0.07, which is the largest effect observed. Fusion (concat 0.629 vs weighted 0.635) and image encoder (ResNet50 0.619 vs ViT-L 0.629) changed accuracy by only about 0.01. Avgpool beat transformer aggregation, and scGPT was clearly worse. Uncertainty: every run so far has been multimodal, so we do not know whether the image branch adds anything or whether most of the performance comes from the scVI RNA embedding. Test: config_005 is RNA-only scVI with multiprofile avgpool, which matches the best configuration except for the image branch and fusion. Comparing it with config_037 directly measures the image modality's contribution. Why now: model setting is a major untested design choice. The result decides whether the remaining budget should go to image-side and fusion variants (if multimodal clearly helps) or to RNA-side and aggregation choices (if RNA alone nearly matches). Further fusion or image-encoder tweaks would mostly re-measure effects already seen to be small.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_037 (scVI + ViT-L, avgpool, weighted fusion) at 0.706 accuracy and 0.667 F1. It beats scVI RNA-only (0.650) and all PCA and scGPT variants, so the RNA encoder appears to matter most. Fusion (weighted slightly above concat) and aggregation (avgpool above transformer) each have some, if thin, evidence. However, all seven experiments used multiprofile, so the profile setting is a core design choice with no evidence at all. 2) Test: config_035 keeps the best encoder pair and weighted fusion but switches to singleprofile. This isolates whether pooling across multiple profiles actually drives the gain or whether single profiles do as well. 3) Why now: This closes the largest remaining blind spot while staying anchored to the best region of the space, so the result is informative either way. If multiprofile clearly helps, later experiments can stay in multiprofile and refine fusion and aggregation. If singleprofile matches or beats it, the search direction changes substantially.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_037 (scVI + ViT-L + avgpool + weighted fusion, 0.706 acc, 0.667 F1). It clearly beats the PCA variants and scVI RNA-only (0.650), so the scVI encoder, multiprofile avgpool and weighted fusion all look favourable. The image encoder choice is still unresolved. It has been compared only once, under PCA with concat fusion. There ViT-L had slightly higher accuracy (0.629 vs 0.619) but ResNet50 had higher F1 (0.610 vs 0.599), so the comparison is effectively a tie. Transformer aggregation already underperformed avgpool once, which makes config_039 less attractive. 2) Test: config_031 keeps the best setting fixed (scVI, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted) and swaps ViT-L for ResNet50. This isolates the image encoder effect in the strongest context. 3) Why now: It resolves a weakly supported design choice and still has a realistic chance of matching or beating the current best. That balances exploitation and uncertainty reduction better than retesting an aggregation choice that has already shown worse results.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_037 (scVI + ViT-L + avgpool + weighted fusion), at 0.706 accuracy and 0.667 F1. It beats the scVI RNA-only baseline (0.650) and the ResNet50 version (0.678), so scVI, ViT-L, multiprofile input and weighted fusion all look favorable. Aggregation is the least resolved choice. Transformer was tested only once, with PCA and concat fusion (config_026), where it scored 0.599 against 0.629 for avgpool. That is a single comparison in a weaker setting, so it is not conclusive. 2. Test: config_039 keeps the best setup and changes only avgpool to transformer. This isolates whether learned attention over multiple profiles helps once stronger scVI embeddings and weighted fusion are used. 3. Why this experiment: it extends the leading configuration, so it could plausibly set a new best. It also settles an important design choice that currently rests on one weak data point. A fusion check (concat versus weighted with scVI) seems less urgent, since the earlier fusion difference was small and consistently favored weighted.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so we have no information on whether multimodal fusion beats single-modality models, whether multiprofile aggregation helps, or which encoders work best. 2) What this tests: config_030 is a central, moderate-complexity anchor. It is multimodal, multiprofile with avgpool aggregation, scVI RNA embeddings, ResNet50 image features and concat fusion. On each axis it uses the simpler or mid-range option. Its result gives a baseline for the most likely high-value region of the space, and later experiments can vary one factor at a time from it: modality ablations (config_005, config_011), aggregation (config_032), fusion (config_031) and encoders (config_018, config_042, config_036). 3) Why it is the best use of the first experiment: starting from a central, plausibly strong configuration makes each later one-factor contrast directly interpretable. It also lets us find early whether combining modalities and profiles is worthwhile, without committing at the outset to the most complex transformer and large-encoder settings.

1. Evidence: Only one experiment is complete. config_030 (multimodal, scVI RNA + ResNet50 image, avgpool, concat) gives a baseline of 0.632 accuracy and 0.607 F1. We do not yet know which of its components drives that performance. 2. What this tests: config_005 keeps the same scVI encoder, multiprofile setting and avgpool aggregation but drops the image modality. Because only one factor changes, it is a clean ablation of whether adding images (and fusing them) improves on RNA alone. 3. Why now: Most of the remaining search space is multimodal. Learning early whether images add value tells us whether to spend the budget on image-encoder and fusion choices or on RNA-side choices such as encoder and aggregation. That makes this the most uncertainty-reducing next step.

1. Evidence: with scvi_n200, multiprofile input and avgpool, adding ResNet50 images through concat fusion scored lower (0.632 acc, 0.607 F1) than RNA alone (0.650 acc, 0.628 F1). That gap is small and comes from one comparison, so it is unclear whether images add little signal or whether simple concatenation lets the noisier image features dilute the RNA signal. 2. Test: config_031 changes only the fusion from concat to weighted and keeps everything else identical to config_030. This isolates the effect of fusion. If weighted fusion matches or beats RNA-only, the multimodal deficit was a fusion problem. If it still trails, image features are probably not adding value under this setup. 3. Why now: most of the untested configurations are multimodal. Knowing early whether the multimodal branch is worth pursuing, and which fusion to use there, shapes many later choices. A single controlled one-variable change gives a clean answer and also has a real chance of producing a new best result.

1) Evidence: with scvi_n200, ResNet50 and avgpool held fixed, weighted fusion (acc 0.678, F1 0.646) beat RNA-only (0.650) and concat fusion (0.632). F1 shows the same order. This suggests weighted fusion is what makes the image modality help, though it rests on single runs. Aggregation has only ever been avgpool, so its effect is completely untested. 2) This experiment changes one variable from the current best: avgpool becomes transformer aggregation, keeping scvi_n200, ResNet50 and weighted fusion. Any difference can then be credited to how multiple profiles are combined. 3) It is the best use of the next run because it builds on the strongest result so far while answering a major open question in the design. 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Within scVI + ResNet50 multiprofile models, two design choices have consistent single-factor evidence. The biggest open question is that every run so far is multimodal, so we don't know how much the image branch actually adds on top of a strong RNA encoder. 2) This experiment: config_005 is RNA-only scVI with multiprofile avgpool, the RNA-only counterpart of the current best config_037.
