If it falls well short, multimodal fusion is confirmed as worthwhile, and the image encoder and fusion should be refined around the scVI backbone. 3) Why now: this ablation resolves the most fundamental design question with one run. Further small tweaks to fusion or image encoder would likely produce marginal, hard-to-interpret differences.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_037 (scVI + ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion; acc 0.706, F1 0.667). It clearly beats PCA and scGPT counterparts and the scVI RNA-only baseline (0.650), so scVI with ViT-L and weighted fusion looks strong. Uncertainty: every experiment so far has used multiprofile, so the profile setting is a completely untested design dimension. 2. Test: config_035 keeps the best configuration and changes only the profile setting to singleprofile. This is a controlled comparison that shows whether aggregating multiple profiles is responsible for the gains or whether single-profile inputs are competitive or better. 3. Why now: Other open questions have at least partial evidence. Transformer aggregation underperformed avgpool once, and concat versus weighted favored weighted. The profile setting has none, and it is a top-level design choice that shapes what else is worth exploring, so resolving it reduces the most uncertainty per experiment. It also stays close to the best region, so it may still perform well.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: Several choices already have fairly clear evidence. Multiprofile with avgpool beats singleprofile (0.706 vs 0.537). scVI is the strongest RNA encoder (0.706, compared with 0.635 for PCA and 0.518 for scGPT). Weighted fusion edged out concat (0.635 vs 0.629). Fusing images adds about 5.6 points over scVI RNA-only (0.706 vs 0.650). The image encoder is still unresolved. Its only comparison, under PCA with concat fusion, gave a small accuracy edge to ViT-L (0.629 vs 0.619) but higher F1 to ResNet50 (0.610 vs 0.599). 2. What this tests: config_031 keeps the best setup (scVI, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion) and swaps only ViT-L for ResNet50. This isolates the image-encoder effect in the context that matters most. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: It resolves the most ambiguous remaining choice. It also has a real chance of beating the current best, given ResNet50's F1 advantage. Testing transformer aggregation instead looks less valuable, since its one comparison already showed it hurting (0.599 vs 0.629).

1) Evidence: scVI is clearly the strongest RNA encoder. config_037 (scVI + ViT-L, avgpool, weighted) reached 0.706 accuracy and 0.667 F1, the best so far. Multiprofile aggregation beats singleprofile by a wide margin (0.706 vs 0.537). How to aggregate profiles is still uncertain. Transformer aggregation has been tried only once, in the weaker PCA + ViT-L + concat setting, where it underperformed avgpool (0.599 vs 0.629). A single comparison in a weaker RNA setting is not enough to rule out an important choice. 2) Test: config_039 changes only the aggregation (avgpool to transformer) relative to the current best. It isolates whether learned cross-profile attention helps once the RNA embeddings are higher quality (scVI rather than PCA) and fusion is weighted. 3) Why now: aggregation is a high-impact design decision, given the large multiprofile vs singleprofile gap, and its evidence is the sparsest. The fusion comparison (config_036) is lower priority because the earlier weighted vs concat difference was small (0.635 vs 0.629). If config_039 wins, it sets a new best. If it loses again, transformer aggregation can be dropped across encoders, saving budget.

1. Evidence: no experiments have been run, so we know nothing yet about which modality, RNA or image encoder, profile setting, aggregation or fusion matters. 2. What it tests: config_030 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200 + resnet50, avgpool, concat) is a central anchor. It uses a mid-complexity RNA encoder, the simpler image backbone, the simplest multiprofile aggregation and the simplest fusion. It is likely to perform reasonably, and each factor can later be changed one at a time against it: rna_only or image_only, singleprofile, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion, pca or scgpt, ViT-L. 3. Why it is the best use of the budget: starting from a central multimodal configuration gives a useful reference point and possibly a strong early result. Starting at an extreme corner such as a unimodal single-profile baseline would leave more of the design space far away, so later single-factor comparisons would be less direct.

1. Evidence: Only one run exists so far. config_030 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI + ResNet50, avgpool, concat) reached 0.632 accuracy and 0.607 F1. A single result cannot show which design choices drive that performance. The most basic open question is whether the image modality adds anything beyond RNA. 2. What this tests: config_005 removes only the image branch and keeps everything else the same (scVI, multiprofile, avgpool). This is a clean one-factor ablation. If accuracy drops clearly, multimodal fusion is valuable, and later runs should focus on image encoder, fusion and aggregation choices. If accuracy is similar or higher, the image branch adds little, and the search should focus on RNA encoders and aggregation. 3. Why it is the best next step: The modality choice decides which part of the 50-configuration space is worth exploring. Settling it first reduces uncertainty more than tuning a secondary factor such as fusion type or aggregation.

1. Evidence: The two completed runs share the scVI RNA encoder, multiprofile input and average pooling. RNA-only (0.650 accuracy, 0.628 F1) slightly beats multimodal concat with ResNet50 (0.632 accuracy, 0.607 F1). That gap is small and comes from single runs, so it is weak evidence that the image branch adds little under naive concat fusion. The aggregation method is completely untested. 2. Test: Swap average pooling for transformer aggregation on the current best setup (RNA-only, scVI, multiprofile), changing only that one factor. This shows whether learned attention over profiles beats simple averaging. 3. Why now: Aggregation affects every multiprofile configuration, unimodal or multimodal, so the answer narrows a large part of the remaining space. Building on the best configuration so far also gives a fair chance of a new top result, which balances exploiting the leading direction with resolving a major open design choice.

1) Evidence and uncertainty: RNA-only scVI multiprofile models score about 0.65 accuracy whether they use avgpool (0.650) or transformer (0.653), so aggregation appears to matter little. Adding ResNet50 images with concat fusion (config_030) lowered accuracy to 0.632, with F1 also lower (0.607 vs ~0.628). It is unclear whether images add nothing or whether naive concatenation lets a noisier image signal hurt performance. 2) What this tests: config_031 keeps everything from config_030 the same except it swaps concat for weighted fusion. This isolates the effect of fusion strategy and shows whether learned modality weighting can recover or exceed the RNA-only baseline. 3) Why this is the best next use of budget: whether multimodality helps is the central design question, and fusion is the most likely reason for the current drop. A single-variable comparison gives a clean answer. If weighted fusion closes the gap, the many weighted-fusion multimodal configurations become worth exploring. If it does not, effort should shift toward RNA encoder choice (scGPT, PCA) or image encoder choice (ViT-L).

1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_031 (multimodal, scVI, ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion), at 0.678 accuracy and 0.646 F1. It beats concat fusion by about 4.6 points and RNA-only by about 2.5 points. That is fairly strong evidence that weighted fusion makes multimodality worthwhile. Transformer aggregation gave only a negligible gain in the RNA-only runs (+0.003), so it is weak evidence. The image encoder is completely untested: every multimodal run so far used ResNet50. 2. What this tests: config_037 changes only the image encoder to ImageNet ViT-L and keeps the best configuration otherwise. Any difference can then be attributed directly to the image backbone. 3. Why it is the best next step: The image encoder is a large, unexplored design choice that could plausibly shift performance more than the aggregation tweak. The experiment also has a reasonable chance of beating the current best. It therefore balances exploration of a major factor with exploitation of the proven weighted-fusion setup.

1) Evidence: weighted fusion beat concat (0.678 vs 0.632 with ResNet50), and ImageNet ViT-L beat ResNet50 under weighted fusion (0.706 vs 0.678, with F1 agreeing). The current best is config_037 (scVI, ViT-L, avgpool, weighted). Aggregation looks less important so far: transformer and avgpool were nearly identical in the RNA-only runs (0.653 vs 0.650). The RNA encoder is still completely unexplored, since every run used scVI. 2) This experiment keeps the best-known setup (ViT-L, avgpool, weighted fusion, multiprofile) and changes only scVI to scGPT. That isolates the effect of the RNA encoder in the strongest context. 3) It is the best use of the budget because it addresses the largest remaining uncertainty while staying close to the top configuration. If the foundation-model RNA embedding helps, it could set a new best. If not, it supports scVI and lets later runs focus on aggregation (e.g., config_039).

1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_037 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted fusion; acc 0.706, F1 0.667). Two comparisons there suggest that weighted fusion and the ViT-L image encoder both help. The RNA encoder appears to matter most: swapping scvi_n200 for scGPT in the same setup dropped accuracy to 0.542. Aggregation looks minor, since transformer and avgpool differed by only about 0.003 in the RNA-only runs. The third RNA encoder, pca_n2000, has never been tested. 2. What this tests: config_025 keeps the best setup fixed and swaps only scvi_n200 for pca_n2000. This cleanly shows whether scVI is truly the best RNA encoder or whether a simpler PCA representation matches or beats it. 3. Why now: The RNA encoder is the design choice with the largest observed effect and the largest unexplored gap. A single controlled experiment resolves it, and the result could either confirm scVI or reveal a stronger direction. That is better use of the budget than tuning aggregation, which so far has shown little effect.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_037 (scVI + ViT-L, avgpool, weighted; acc 0.706, F1 0.667). Three findings point to it. Weighted fusion beat concat with ResNet50 (+0.046). ViT-L beat ResNet50 (+0.029). scVI clearly beat PCA and scGPT. Aggregation remains the main untested choice in the multimodal setting. In RNA-only runs, transformer was only slightly better than avgpool (0.653 vs 0.650), but that gap may widen when image features from several profiles must be combined. 2) This run changes only the aggregation (avgpool to transformer) in the best configuration. That is a controlled test of whether learned set aggregation adds value on top of the strongest encoders and fusion. 3) It is the best use of budget because it both exploits the strongest direction, with a real chance of a new best, and answers an important open design question with a clean one-variable comparison. Single-profile and unimodal baselines can be tested later.

1) Evidence: Every completed run used multiprofile, so the profile-setting choice is completely untested. The other dimensions have useful signal. Weighted fusion beat concat with resnet50 (0.678 vs 0.632). ViT-L beat resnet50 (0.706 vs 0.678). scVI clearly beat PCA (0.635) and scGPT (0.542). Transformer aggregation gave a modest gain over avgpool (0.725 vs 0.706), consistent with a small gain in the RNA-only runs. 2) Test: config_035 runs singleprofile inside the best-known setup (scVI + ViT-L + weighted fusion). Compared against config_037 and config_039, it shows whether aggregating multiple profiles is responsible for much of the performance. 3) Why now: Further tuning of fusion or aggregation would likely give only small gains along directions we already partly understand. This run closes the largest remaining gap in our knowledge. If singleprofile is competitive, it opens a cheaper branch of the search space. If it is clearly worse, it confirms that we should concentrate the remaining budget on multiprofile variants.

Evidence: the best result so far is config_039 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. Several design choices already have supporting comparisons: multiprofile beat singleprofile (0.706 vs 0.537), scvi_n200 beat pca_n2000 and scgpt, ViT-L beat ResNet50, weighted fusion beat concat, and transformer aggregation gave a small gain. The biggest gap is that no image-only model has been run. RNA-only reaches about 0.65, but it is unknown how much of the multimodal gain comes from ViT-L image features alone. What it tests: image-only ViT-L with transformer aggregation, in the same multiprofile setup as the best model. It shows whether fusing RNA adds value beyond strong image features, or whether the image branch drives most of the performance. Why now: this is the most important unresolved question, the role of each modality, and no multimodal fusion variant can answer it. The other candidate was config_038 (concat fusion in the best setup). I ranked it lower because weighted fusion already has one supporting comparison, so it would mostly fine-tune a choice with some evidence. A single image-only run removes a major uncertainty and guides later decisions about fusion and RNA encoders.

1. Evidence: no experiments have been run, so I have no information about which design choices matter. 2. What it tests: this is a central anchor configuration. It uses multimodal input, multiprofile inputs and the mid-range scvi_n200 RNA encoder. It pairs these with the stronger-prior imagenet_vit_l image encoder and the simplest aggregation (avgpool) and fusion (concat) options. Because it sits in the middle of the design space, each later run can change one factor at a time and be compared directly against it. Those factors are: unimodal vs. multimodal (config_005, config_014), single vs. multiprofile (config_034), avgpool vs. transformer (config_038), concat vs. weighted (config_037), and the RNA or image encoder (config_024, config_048, config_030). 3. Why it is the best use of the first run: with a limited budget, a central anchor that is also plausibly high-performing gives a useful accuracy and F1 reference point. It also sets up efficient one-factor ablations, rather than starting at an extreme corner such as a minimal unimodal baseline.

1) Evidence: we have only one result so far. The multimodal, multiprofile config_036 (scVI + ViT-L, avgpool, concat) reached 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. With a single data point, we cannot tell which component drives this performance. 2) Test: config_005 keeps everything identical except that it removes the image branch (RNA-only scVI, multiprofile, avgpool). This is a clean one-factor ablation of whether the image modality adds value over RNA. 3) Why now: whether to use multimodal models at all is the most consequential design choice. It decides whether the budget should go to image encoder and fusion variants, or to RNA encoders and aggregation. Settling it early, with a controlled comparison, best focuses the remaining experiments.

1. Evidence: Adding imagenet_vit_l images to scvi_n200 RNA (multimodal, avgpool, concat) raised accuracy from 0.650 to 0.715, and F1 rose in parallel (0.628 to 0.687). So multimodality looks clearly useful. However, aggregation has only been tested with avgpool, so its effect is completely unknown. 2. Test: config_038 changes just one factor of the current best setup, swapping avgpool for transformer aggregation, while keeping the scvi_n200 encoder, the vit_l encoder, multiprofile and concat fusion fixed. This cleanly isolates whether learned attention over multiple profiles beats simple mean pooling. 3. Why now: aggregation affects a large share of the remaining multiprofile configurations, so resolving it narrows the search a lot. It also extends the best-performing direction found so far, giving a good chance of an immediate gain while reducing uncertainty about a major design choice.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: Multimodal scVI + ViT-L clearly beats RNA-only scVI, about 0.72 vs 0.65 accuracy, so the image modality adds value. Transformer and avgpool aggregation are nearly tied (+0.006 accuracy but -0.006 F1), so aggregation looks like a minor factor. Fusion strategy has never been varied; every multimodal run used concat. 2. What this tests: config_039 keeps the best configuration so far (config_038) and changes only concat to weighted fusion. This isolates the effect of fusion on the strongest backbone found so far. 3. Why it is the best next step: It exploits the promising multimodal direction while resolving an untested design choice that bears directly on how the two modalities are combined. Encoder swaps (scGPT, ResNet50) remain the next open questions after this.

1. Evidence: All four completed runs use the scVI RNA encoder. The three multimodal runs (scVI + ViT-L) differ only in aggregation and fusion, and their accuracies fall in a narrow band (0.715 to 0.725). Their F1 scores are also close and do not rank the same way (avgpool+concat has the highest F1). So aggregation and fusion look like second-order choices. Multimodal clearly beats RNA-only (0.650), so the image modality matters. The largest untested uncertainty is the choice of encoders. 2. Test: This run keeps the current best setting (multiprofile, ViT-L, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) and swaps only the RNA encoder from scVI to scGPT. That gives a clean one-factor comparison against config_039 and shows whether the foundation-model RNA embedding adds or loses accuracy. 3. Why now: Spending more budget on aggregation or fusion within scVI + ViT-L would yield little new information. A different encoder could shift performance far more than the differences seen so far. Testing it inside the best known setting also keeps a good chance of improving on the current best.

1. Evidence: The RNA encoder looks like the most sensitive design choice so far. Swapping scvi_n200 for scgpt in the best setup (multiprofile, vit_l, transformer, weighted) dropped accuracy from 0.725 to 0.520. By contrast, the aggregation and fusion changes moved accuracy by only about 0.01, with mixed F1 results. pca_n2000 has not been tested in any setting, so we cannot yet say whether scvi_n200 is the best RNA representation or just better than scgpt. 2. What it tests: config_027 changes only the RNA encoder (pca_n2000 instead of scvi_n200) and keeps everything else from the current best configuration. This cleanly isolates the effect of the RNA encoder. 3. Why now: the RNA encoder has shown the largest effect, and PCA could plausibly match or beat scVI. Resolving this choice is worth more than further small aggregation or fusion tweaks, and it could also yield a new best configuration. The image encoder (resnet50) and the single-profile setting remain good follow-up ablations.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: scvi_n200 is clearly the strongest RNA encoder so far (about 0.72 accuracy, versus 0.59 for pca_n2000 and 0.52 for scgpt in the same setup). Multimodal beats rna_only (0.715 vs 0.650). The aggregation and fusion variants with scvi and ViT-L differ by under 0.01 in accuracy, with F1 not consistently favouring any of them, so those choices look minor. The image encoder is a major design axis that has not been tested: every multimodal run used imagenet_vit_l. 2. What this tests: config_033 keeps the best-performing context (scvi_n200, multiprofile, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) and swaps only the image encoder to resnet50. This isolates the effect of image encoder choice in the most relevant setting. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: it directly reduces uncertainty about a high-impact, unexplored factor. It also stays in a promising region, so it could match or beat the current best of 0.725. Further aggregation or fusion tweaks would likely yield only small differences.

1. Evidence: scvi_n200 is clearly the strongest RNA encoder. It beat pca_n2000 (0.586) and scgpt (0.520), and multimodal beat RNA-only (0.715 vs 0.650). Within scvi multiprofile runs, the aggregation, fusion and image-encoder choices differ by only about 0.01 in accuracy (0.713–0.725), with F1 rankings that are mixed. Those differences are too small to resolve further with single runs. The profile setting is a major design choice that has never been tested: every completed run is multiprofile. 2. This experiment keeps the best setup (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + weighted fusion) and switches to singleprofile, making it a direct comparison with config_039 (0.725). It will show how much multiprofile aggregation actually contributes, which also indicates whether aggregation choices are worth tuning further. 3. Under a limited budget, resolving an entirely unexplored, high-level factor is more informative than fine-tuning the small aggregation/fusion differences, while staying in the strongest encoder region keeps the result relevant for exploitation.

1) Evidence: The scVI + ViT-L multiprofile models are clearly strongest. Accuracy ranges from 0.715 to 0.725 across avgpool/transformer aggregation and concat/weighted fusion, so those choices look like small, possibly noise-level effects. RNA encoder and multiprofile setting matter much more: scGPT and PCA drop to 0.52-0.59, and singleprofile drops to 0.54. RNA-only scVI reaches 0.650, but there is no image-only baseline, so we do not know how much the gain comes from the image modality versus true multimodal complementarity. 2) Test: An image-only ViT-L model with transformer aggregation in the multiprofile setting, matched to the best multimodal setup (config_039). It shows whether ViT-L image features alone approach about 0.72, meaning RNA adds little, or fall well below, meaning fusion is essential. Together with the existing RNA-only result, it cleanly measures each modality's contribution. 3) Why now: Further aggregation/fusion variants (e.g., config_037) would likely land within the current noise band and teach little. This baseline resolves a major open question about modality contribution and will guide whether remaining budget goes to image-encoder choices, RNA-side choices, or fusion refinements.

1. Evidence: The scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l multimodal multiprofile family is clearly the strongest. scGPT, PCA, image-only and single-profile runs all fall far below it. Within that family, three of the four aggregation × fusion combinations are tested: avgpool/concat 0.715, transformer/concat 0.721 and transformer/weighted 0.725 (the best). The gaps are small (~0.5 pts), and F1 does not follow accuracy: avgpool/concat has the highest F1 of the three at 0.687. So it is still unclear whether aggregation or fusion actually matters. 2. Test: avgpool + weighted fusion completes the 2×2 factorial with the best encoders. That separates the main effect of fusion from the main effect of aggregation and shows whether they interact. It could also uncover a simpler configuration that matches or beats the current best. 3. Why now: it targets the remaining uncertainty in the top-performing region while staying close to the best configuration. Under a limited budget, that makes it both informative and a reasonable bet for high accuracy.

1) No experiments have been run, so there is no evidence on any design choice: modality, single vs. multi-profile, RNA encoder, image encoder, aggregation or fusion. 2) This run sets a central anchor that combines both modalities, multiple profiles, mid-capacity choices for both encoders (scVI RNA, ImageNet ViT-L image) and the simplest options for aggregation (avgpool) and fusion (concat). It tells us early whether the full multimodal, multi-profile pipeline performs well. 3) An anchor like this is a better use of the first run than an extreme baseline. Each later run can change one factor against it: drop to RNA-only or image-only (config_005 or config_014), switch to single-profile (config_034), use transformer aggregation (config_038), use weighted fusion (config_037), or swap an encoder (config_030, config_048). Those one-factor contrasts let us find which choices matter at the lowest experiment cost, while starting from a configuration with a reasonable chance of strong validation accuracy.

1. Evidence: There is only one result so far. The multimodal scVI + ViT-L model with avgpool and concat fusion reached 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. We have no baseline, so we cannot tell whether the image modality adds anything. 2. Test: config_005 keeps the same RNA encoder (scvi_n200), multiprofile setting and avgpool aggregation, and drops only the image branch. This isolates how much the image modality contributes. 3. Why now: Whether multimodal fusion beats RNA-only is the most important structural question, since it governs most of the remaining search space (36 of the 50 untested configurations are multimodal). Answering it with a clean one-factor ablation tells us where to spend the budget next: on image encoder and fusion choices if images help, or on RNA encoder and aggregation choices if they do not. That makes it more informative than tuning aggregation or fusion within an unverified multimodal setup.

Evidence: with the RNA encoder (scVI) and aggregation (avgpool) held fixed, multimodal concat with ViT-L (0.715 acc, 0.687 F1) beats RNA-only (0.650 acc, 0.628 F1). That 6.5-point gain is promising but comes from a single pair of runs. It is also unclear whether the gain comes from combining modalities or from the image features alone. Question: running image-only ViT-L with the same multiprofile avgpool setting completes a matched modality ablation. It shows whether images alone match or beat the multimodal model, which would mean RNA adds little. It also shows whether fusion gives real gains over both single modalities. Why now: modality choice is the most important design decision so far. This one run clarifies whether later runs should focus on fusion, aggregation and RNA-encoder choices within multimodal models, or on image-encoder choices. That is a better use of budget than tuning aggregation or fusion before the source of the gain is known.

1. Evidence: The three completed runs share scVI RNA, ViT-L images, avgpool and multiprofile. Within that setup, multimodal concat (0.715 acc / 0.687 F1) beat RNA-only (0.650) and image-only (0.332). So combining modalities helps, and RNA carries most of the signal. Aggregation, fusion and encoder choice have not been varied at all. 2. Test: config_038 keeps the best configuration fixed and changes only avgpool to transformer aggregation. This isolates whether learned attention over multiple profiles beats simple mean pooling. 3. Why now: Aggregation is likely a high-impact choice for multiprofile models, and a one-factor change from the current best gives a clean comparison. It also has a reasonable chance of improving accuracy. The result will guide later tests of fusion (weighted vs concat) and RNA encoder (scGPT vs PCA).

1. Evidence: multimodal (0.715-0.721) clearly beats RNA-only (0.650) and image-only (0.332). RNA is the dominant signal source. The avgpool vs transformer comparison is inconclusive: transformer has slightly higher accuracy (+0.006) but lower F1. The RNA encoder, the image encoder, fusion and profile setting are all still untested. 2. This experiment changes only one factor from config_036, swapping scvi_n200 for scGPT while keeping vit_l, multiprofile, avgpool and concat. It isolates whether a foundation-model RNA embedding improves on scVI. 3. Because RNA carries most of the predictive signal, the RNA encoder is likely the highest-impact unexplored choice. A one-factor change gives a clean comparison and could also raise the performance ceiling. Fusion type and aggregation can be refined later on top of whichever RNA encoder wins.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: Multimodal scVI + ViT-L with concat fusion is the strongest setup so far (0.715–0.721 accuracy). It clearly beats RNA-only (0.650) and image-only (0.332). scVI also clearly beats scGPT (0.518). Avgpool and transformer aggregation look roughly equivalent: transformer has slightly higher accuracy but slightly lower F1, so the difference is too small to call. Fusion method is a whole design dimension that has never been tested, because every multimodal run used concat. 2. What this tests: config_037 matches the best avgpool baseline (config_036) except for fusion, swapping concat for weighted. This gives a clean one-variable comparison of fusion strategy. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: it resolves the largest untested factor in the most promising region of the search space. It could plausibly improve on the current best, and its result will show whether fusion is worth exploring further with the other encoders and aggregations.

Evidence: multimodal scVI + ViT-L is clearly the strongest direction (about 0.71-0.72 accuracy, versus 0.65 for RNA-only and 0.33 for image-only). Changing aggregation (avgpool vs transformer) or fusion (concat vs weighted) moved results by only about 0.01, so neither appears to matter much. The RNA encoder, by contrast, matters a lot: swapping scVI for scGPT dropped accuracy to 0.52. Since RNA carries most of the signal, the most important open question is whether the untested PCA_n2000 RNA encoder matches or beats scVI. Test: config_024 keeps the reference setup (multiprofile, ViT-L, avgpool, concat) and changes only the RNA encoder to PCA. This gives a clean comparison with config_036 (scVI) and config_048 (scGPT), completing the RNA encoder comparison under fixed conditions. Why now: the encoder choice has shown far larger effects than aggregation or fusion tweaks. Resolving it is a better use of the limited budget than fine-tuning the current best, and it could reveal a stronger configuration.

1. Evidence: scVI is clearly the strongest RNA encoder tested (0.715 accuracy vs 0.629 for PCA and 0.518 for scGPT in the same multimodal setup). Adding images on top of scVI gives about a 6.5-point gain over RNA-only (0.715 vs 0.650). Aggregation and fusion changes made only small, mixed differences: the transformer was +0.006 accuracy but had lower F1, and weighted fusion was slightly worse. However, every image-containing run so far used imagenet_vit_l, and image-only ViT-L performs poorly (0.33). The image encoder is therefore a completely untested and plausibly important design choice. 2. This experiment swaps only the image encoder to resnet50 inside the best-known scVI/multiprofile/avgpool/concat setup, matching config_036. It isolates whether a different image representation changes how much the image modality contributes. 3. More aggregation or fusion tweaks would likely give small, noisy differences. A controlled test of the image encoder addresses the largest remaining uncertainty, and it could also produce a new best configuration, so it balances exploration and exploitation under the limited budget.

1) Evidence: scvi_n200 is clearly the strongest RNA encoder, ahead of PCA at 0.629 and scGPT at 0.518. imagenet_vit_l clearly beats resnet50 (0.715 vs 0.632). Multimodal beats RNA-only by about 6.5 points. Aggregation (avgpool 0.715 vs transformer 0.721, with F1 favoring avgpool) and fusion (concat 0.715 vs weighted 0.706) show only small differences, likely within noise. However, every experiment so far has used multiprofile, so whether multiprofile aggregation helps at all is completely untested. 2) This run uses the best-known setup (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + concat) in singleprofile mode. It directly measures the value of multiprofile aggregation, a major architectural choice. 3) Further aggregation or fusion tweaks such as config_039 would likely give only marginal, noisy gains. Resolving the largest untested design dimension on the strongest backbone is the most informative use of the limited budget, and it still has a reasonable chance of competitive performance.

Evidence: the scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + multiprofile combination clearly dominates. Swapping in other RNA encoders (scgpt 0.518, pca 0.629), switching to resnet50 (0.632), or using singleprofile (0.532) each costs 9 to 20 points. Within this best region, transformer+concat scored 0.721, avgpool+concat 0.715 and avgpool+weighted 0.706. These are small differences, and F1 favors avgpool+concat, so the aggregation and fusion choices remain uncertain. Test: config_039 (transformer+weighted) is the only missing cell of the 2x2 aggregation × fusion grid in this best region. It shows whether weighted fusion consistently underperforms concat or interacts with transformer aggregation. Why now: it exploits the strongest direction while resolving the remaining open design question there. That is a better use of the limited budget than revisiting regions that have already been clearly ruled out.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: we have one result, config_030 (multimodal, scvi_n200 + resnet50, avgpool, concat), at 0.632 validation accuracy and 0.607 F1. 1. Evidence: Only two experiments exist. RNA-only scVI with avgpool (0.650 acc, 0.628 F1) slightly beat multimodal scVI+ResNet50 concat with avgpool (0.632 acc, 0.607 F1). 1) Evidence so far: with scvi_n200, RNA-only models (0.650 and 0.653) beat the multimodal concat model with resnet50 (0.632). 1. Evidence: scVI is clearly the stronger RNA encoder (about 0.65 vs 0.51 for scGPT). Aggregation choice barely matters for RNA-only models (avgpool 0.650 vs transformer 0.653). Adding ResNet50 images with concat fusion lowered accuracy to 0.632 (F1 0.607 vs 0.628), so the open question is whether multimodality helps at all. 2. 1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_031 (scVI + ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion), with 0.678 accuracy and 0.646 F1. 1. Evidence: The best run so far is config_037 (scVI + ViT-L, avgpool, weighted fusion) at 0.706 accuracy and 0.667 F1. Two changes each helped on their own: weighted fusion beat concat (0.678 vs 0.632 with ResNet50), and ViT-L beat ResNet50 (0.706 vs 0.678). The main open question is aggregation. It has only been compared in the RNA-only setting, where transformer and avgpool were nearly tied (0.653 vs 0.650), so we do not know whether transformer aggregation helps when two modalities are fused. 2. 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_039 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion; acc 0.725, F1 0.685). 1. Evidence: Every completed run used multiprofile. Within that setting the findings are fairly consistent: scVI beats PCA and scGPT, ViT-L beats ResNet50, and weighted fusion beats concat. Why now: The remaining budget should not go on small refinements of an axis we have never questioned. 1) Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_039 (scVI + ViT-L, transformer, weighted fusion; 0.725 acc, 0.685 F1). 1. Evidence and uncertainty: there is only one result so far. config_030 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI + ResNet50, avgpool, concat) reached 0.632 validation accuracy and 0.607 F1. 1. Evidence: Only two runs exist. Adding ResNet50 image features to scVI RNA with concat fusion (config_030, acc 0.632, F1 0.607) did slightly worse than RNA-only (config_005, acc 0.650, F1 0.628). Test: config_031 is identical to config_030 except it uses weighted fusion instead of concat. This isolates the fusion effect. Evidence: with scvi_n200, ResNet50 and avgpool held fixed, weighted fusion (0.678 acc / 0.646 F1) beat concat (0.632 / 0.607) and also beat RNA-only (0.650 / 0.628). Evidence: with scVI fixed, weighted fusion beat concat (0.678 vs 0.632), transformer aggregation beat avgpool (0.713 vs 0.678), and ViT-L was slightly ahead of ResNet50 in accuracy (0.725 vs 0.713) but slightly behind in F1. 1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_039 (scVI + ViT-L + transformer + weighted, 0.725 accuracy). Transformer aggregation and weighted fusion have each helped in controlled comparisons. 1. Evidence and uncertainty: scVI is clearly the best RNA encoder so far (0.725 vs 0.586 for PCA and 0.520 for scGPT). Transformer aggregation gave a large gain over avgpool (0.678 to 0.713 with ResNet50 and weighted fusion). Why it is the best use of budget: if RNA-only with a transformer approaches about 0.72, the image branch adds little and later experiments should focus on RNA and aggregation choices. Either outcome changes how the remaining experiments are allocated more than a small tweak near the current optimum would.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: Only one experiment has been run. config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA RNA, ResNet50, avgpool, concat) gave 0.619 accuracy and 0.610 F1. With a single data point, we do not yet know which design factor drives performance. 2.
